Task: A student measures the specific heat capacity of a metal block.
Steps:
Measure the mass of the block with a balance.
Put a heater and a thermometer into the block and wrap it in insulation.
Record the starting temperature, then switch on the heater and start a timer.
After 10 minutes, switch off and record the highest temperature reached.
Calculate the energy supplied from the power of the heater and the time.
Calculate the specific heat capacity: energy ÷ (mass × temperature rise).

Task: A student compares how well different materials insulate a beaker of hot water.
Steps:
Wrap a beaker in one of the insulating materials.
Pour in a measured volume of hot water and fit a lid with a thermometer.
Record the starting temperature and start a stopwatch.
Record the temperature again after 10 minutes.
Repeat with each material, using the same volume and starting temperature of water.
Compare the temperature falls: the smallest fall shows the best insulator.

Practical: Resistance and the length of a wire
Task: A student investigates how the length of a wire affects its resistance.
Steps:
Connect the wire in a circuit, with an ammeter in series and a voltmeter across the wire.
Attach the crocodile clips 10 cm apart on the wire.
Switch on and record the current and the potential difference.
Switch off to let the wire cool, then move the clips to 20 cm apart.
Repeat the readings for a range of lengths.
Calculate the resistance for each length and plot resistance against length.

Practical: Resistors in series and in parallel
Task: A student compares the total resistance of two resistors in series and in parallel.
Steps:
Connect the two resistors in series with a power supply and an ammeter.
Connect a voltmeter across both resistors.
Switch on, record the current and the potential difference, then switch off.
Calculate the total resistance using R = V ÷ I.
Reconnect the two resistors in parallel and take the readings again.
Compare the two values of total resistance.

Practical: I–V characteristic of a filament lamp
Task: A student finds the I–V characteristic of a filament lamp.
Steps:
Connect the lamp in series with a power supply, a variable resistor and an ammeter.
Connect a voltmeter in parallel with the lamp.
Record the current and the potential difference.
Adjust the variable resistor and record a new pair of readings; do this several times.
Reverse the connections to the power supply and take the readings again.
Plot a graph of current against potential difference.

Task: A student measures the density of a rectangular metal block.
Steps:
Measure the mass of the block with a balance.
Measure the length, width and height of the block with a ruler.
Calculate the volume: length × width × height.
Calculate the density: mass ÷ volume.
Note: The two measuring steps can be done in either order.

Task: A student measures the density of a small stone.
Steps:
Measure the mass of the dry stone with a balance.
Part-fill a measuring cylinder with water and record the volume.
Lower the stone into the water until it is fully covered.
Record the new volume shown on the measuring cylinder.
Subtract the two volumes to find the volume of the stone.
Calculate the density: mass ÷ volume.

Task: A student measures the density of a liquid.
Steps:
Put an empty measuring cylinder on a balance and record its mass.
Pour some of the liquid into the measuring cylinder.
Record the volume of the liquid and the new mass on the balance.
Subtract the two masses to find the mass of the liquid.
Calculate the density: mass ÷ volume.

Practical: Force and extension of a spring
Task: A student investigates how the force on a spring affects its extension.
Steps:
Hang the spring from a clamp stand next to a ruler.
Measure the original length of the spring.
Hang a 1 N weight on the spring and measure its new length.
Calculate the extension: new length − original length.
Add more weights one at a time, finding the extension each time.
Plot a graph of force against extension.

Task: A student investigates how the force on a trolley affects its acceleration.
Steps:
Attach a string to a trolley and pass it over a pulley at the end of the bench.
Hang a mass on the end of the string and hold the trolley still.
Release the trolley so that it passes through two light gates.
Record the acceleration calculated by the data logger.
Move a mass from the trolley to the hanger to increase the force, then repeat.
Plot a graph of acceleration against force.

Task: A student investigates how the mass of a trolley affects its acceleration.
Steps:
Attach a string to a trolley and pass it over a pulley at the end of the bench.
Hang a mass on the end of the string and hold the trolley still.
Release the trolley and record its acceleration using light gates.
Add a mass to the trolley, keeping the hanging mass the same.
Release the trolley again and record the new acceleration.
Repeat for several masses and plot a graph of acceleration against mass.

Task: A student measures the speed of the waves in a ripple tank.
Steps:
Set up the ripple tank with a lamp above it and a white screen below.
Switch on the motor so that the dipper makes steady waves.
Place a ruler on the screen and photograph the wave pattern.
Measure the length of 10 waves on the photograph and divide by 10 to find the wavelength.
Count the waves passing a point in 10 seconds and divide by 10 to find the frequency.
Calculate the wave speed: frequency × wavelength.
Note: The frequency can be found before or after the wavelength.

Task: A student measures the speed of a wave on a stretched string.
Steps:
Attach one end of a string to a vibration generator and pass the other end over a pulley.
Hang masses on the end of the string to keep it taut.
Switch on the signal generator and adjust the frequency until clear loops appear.
Measure the length of several loops and work out the wavelength.
Read the frequency from the signal generator.
Calculate the wave speed: frequency × wavelength.
Note: The frequency can be read before or after the wavelength is measured.

Task: A student compares how much infrared radiation different surfaces emit.
Steps:
Fill a Leslie cube with hot water and put the lid on.
Leave it for a minute so that every face reaches the same temperature.
Hold an infrared detector 10 cm from one face and record the reading.
Repeat for each of the other faces, keeping the detector the same distance away.
Compare the readings: the highest reading shows the best emitter.

Task: A student investigates the refraction of light by a glass block.
Steps:
Place a glass block on a sheet of paper and draw around it.
Shine a narrow ray of light from a ray box at the side of the block.
Mark the path of the ray going in and the ray coming out with crosses.
Remove the block and join the crosses to show the path of the ray through the glass.
Draw the normal at the point where the ray enters the block.
Measure the angle of incidence and the angle of refraction with a protractor.
